# Conditional means and Stein identities for general uniform convex bodies

The coordinate conditional-mean monotonicity used for independent signed
exponentials does not extend to the uniform law on a general convex body.
It fails in dimension two, already for a triangle with integer vertices.
The scalar Stein identity survives, but neither its exponential-specific
conditional-mean representation nor the resulting coefficient bound does.

## 1. A minimal-dimensional rational counterexample

Let

    K=conv{(0,1),(1,0),(0,2)} subset R^2,

and let X be uniform on K. This triangle has area 1/2, so its density
is two. Set T=X_1+X_2. In the coordinates t=T, z=X_1, the inverse
map is (X_1,X_2)=(z,t-z), with absolute Jacobian one. The triangle is
exactly

    1<=t<=2,       0<=z<=2-t.

Hence, for every 1<t<2,

    f_T(t)=2(2-t),
    Law(X_1 | T=t)=Uniform[0,2-t],
    E[X_1 | T=t]=(2-t)/2,
    E[X_2 | T=t]=(3t-2)/2.                             (1)

The first conditional mean is strictly decreasing. The second has slope
3/2, exceeding one. Their sum is t, as it must be. These assertions hold
throughout an open interval of positive density; changing versions at
null conditioning values cannot restore monotonicity.

This is the smallest possible ambient dimension for failure: in dimension
one conditioning X_1 on its own value forces the conditional mean to be
t. The example also has the minimum number of vertices of a full-dimensional
planar polytope. It is a genuine compact full-dimensional convex body, and
all its points have nonnegative coordinates.

The coordinate calculation automatically includes the coarea factor.
In Euclidean section language the line segment has length
sqrt(2)(2-t), while |grad T|=sqrt(2); their quotient is the section
factor 2-t used above.

## 2. What conditional geometry still gives

For a uniform law on any full-dimensional convex body in R^m,
T=sum_i X_i has a positive density on the interior of its projection
interval. Conditioning gives uniform normalized section measure there,
and therefore

    sum_i E[X_i | T=t]=t.                              (2)

The section-volume density is log-concave; for m>=2 its
1/(m-1)-power is concave by Brunn--Minkowski. However (1) shows that
neither log-concavity nor the stronger power concavity forces the
individual means in (2) to be nondecreasing or 1-Lipschitz.

Indeed there is no universal slope bound for individual conditional
means. For any L>0 map the unit square (t,z) in [0,1]^2 to

    X_1=z-Lt,      X_2=(1+L)t-z.

This is an invertible linear map of determinant -1, so it produces a
full-dimensional uniform parallelogram law. Its sum is exactly t and
its conditional means have slopes -L and 1+L. The projection law stays
uniform on [0,1] while those slopes become arbitrarily large in magnitude.

## 3. The surviving one-dimensional Stein identity

Let f be any probability density supported on a bounded interval [a,b],
positive on its interior, and let mu be its mean. Define, for a<t<b,

    tau(t)=[integral_t^b (s-mu)f(s)ds]/f(t)
          =[integral_a^t (mu-s)f(s)ds]/f(t).             (3)

The two numerators agree because the total first centered moment is zero.
The numerator is positive: use the lower integral for t<=mu and the
upper integral for t>=mu. It vanishes at both endpoints. Ordinary
integration by parts therefore proves, for C^1 test functions,

    E[(T-mu)phi(T)]=E[tau(T)phi'(T)],
    (tau f)'=(mu-t)f.                                 (4)

Compact support makes all relevant moments finite. The identity is valid
without independence, and applies to every convex-body projection above.
It is simply the canonical scalar Stein kernel of that projection law.

Where f and tau are differentiable and positive, it gives the exact
logarithmic derivative identity

    f'(t)/f(t)=[mu-t-tau'(t)]/tau(t).                   (5)

By itself (5) gives no upper bound on tau'.

For the triangle in section 1, mu=4/3 and direct calculation gives

    tau(t)=(t-1)(2-t)/3.                               (6)

Substitution verifies (4) and f'/f=-1/(2-t). Both conditional means in
(1) are affine in t, whereas (6) is a nonconstant quadratic polynomial.
Thus this kernel cannot be any fixed linear combination of those two
conditional means, even allowing an additional constant term.

## 4. Stein failure even when both conditional means are monotone

The preceding example already defeats the conditional monotonicity.
A different triangle cleanly separates the independent failure of the
exponential-specific Stein bound. Let

    K'=conv{(-3,3),(3,-3),(3,3)}
       ={x_1<=3, x_2<=3, x_1+x_2>=0}.

Its area is 18. In coordinates t=x_1+x_2, z=x_1 it is

    0<=t<=6,       t-3<=z<=3.

Consequently

    f_T(t)=(6-t)/18,     mu=2,
    E[X_1 | T=t]=E[X_2 | T=t]=t/2,
    tau(t)=t(6-t)/3.                                  (7)

The conditional means are both increasing and 1-Lipschitz. Nonetheless,

    tau'(t)=2-2t/3>1       for 0<t<3/2.

In particular the naive bound tau'<=max_i c_i=1, with coefficients
c_1=c_2=1 in T=X_1+X_2, fails on an open interval. The density is strictly
decreasing throughout (0,6), including (0,1), which lies below mu-1.
So the corresponding exponential mode conclusion also fails. The mode
at zero refers to the right-limit density; the contradiction uses only
strict interior conditioning values and is not a boundary convention.

If nonnegative coordinates are desired, translate K' by (3,3). Its
vertices become (0,6),(6,0),(6,6); the sum is translated by six, the
conditional means remain t/2, and the same failures occur with
f(t)=(12-t)/18 on (6,12), mean eight, and kernel
(t-6)(12-t)/3.

For precision, the different triangle
{x_1,x_2>=0, x_1+x_2<=6} has sum density t/18 and mean four.
It does not have the decreasing density in (7). Reflecting it as above
is essential to the stated mode-bound counterexample.

## 5. Why the signed-exponential argument is different

For independent Z_i=c_i E_i, one-coordinate exponential integration by
parts yields

    E[(Z_i-c_i)phi(sum Z)]
          =E[c_i Z_i phi'(sum Z)].

After summing and conditioning this identifies the actual scalar kernel
as sum_i c_i E[Z_i | sum Z=t]. Independence permits that one-coordinate
identity with the other variables fixed. The log-concavity of the
independent remaining sum then makes the conditional means monotone,
and their unit total slope bounds the kernel derivative by max c_i.

A uniform convex-body law generally has dependent coordinates and boundary
terms in coordinate integration by parts. The kernel identification does
not survive, even when the conditional means happen to be monotone as
in (7). The valid residual statements are (2), projection power concavity,
and the scalar identity (3)--(5). Neither counterexample is an OC
counterexample, and neither weakens the proved independent-exponential
comparison; they prohibit the indicated unproved extension of it.
